(vs. [[1972 Washington Redskins season|Redskins]]) 14–7 | pro_bowlers = {{Collapsible list |title = 9 |1 = SS [[Dick Anderson]] |2 = MLB [[Nick Buoniconti]] |3 = FB [[Larry Csonka]] |4 = T [[Norm Evans]] |5 = G [[Larry Little]] |6 = RB [[Mercury Morris]] |7 = FS [[Jake Scott]] |8 = DE [[Bill Stanfill]] |9 = WR [[Paul Warfield]] }} | AP_All-pros = {{Collapsible list |title = 4 |1 = SS [[Dick Anderson]] |2 = QB [[Earl Morrall]] |3 = G [[Larry Little]] |4 = DE [[Bill Stanfill]] }} | shortnavlink = Dolphins seasons }} [[File:1986 Jeno's Pizza - 33 - Jim Kiick (cropped).jpg|thumb|200px|[[Jim Kiick]] (#21) rushes for Miami in [[Super Bowl VII]]]] The '''1972 Miami Dolphins season''' was the [[Miami Dolphins|franchise's]] seventh season and third in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). The team was led by third-year head coach [[Don Shula]] and achieved the only [[perfect season]] in NFL history (and only the second perfect season in professional football history after the [[1948 Cleveland Browns season|1948 Cleveland Browns]]). The team also led the league in both points scored and fewest points allowed. Starting quarterback [[Bob Griese]] broke his ankle in week 5, leaving backup [[Earl Morrall]] to start the remainder of the regular season, though Griese relieved Morrall in the second half of the AFC Championship Game and started [[Super Bowl VII]]. Morrall, a 38-year-old who spent much of his career backing up stars including [[Johnny Unitas]], was named [[Associated Press NFL Most Valuable Player Award|MVP]] in 1968 under Shula when the pair led the [[1968 Baltimore Colts season|Baltimore Colts]] to the NFL championship. The Dolphins clinched the AFC East title in week 10 with Morrall at quarterback.100 Things Dolphins Fans Should Know and Do Before They Die, Armando Salguero, Triumph Books, Chicago, 2020, ISBN 978-1-62937-722-3, p. 4 None of their regular season opponents advanced to the eight-team [[1972–73 NFL playoffs|postseason]]; three had made the [[1971–72 NFL playoffs|previous postseason]] ([[1972 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City]], [[1972 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota]], [[1972 Baltimore Colts season|Baltimore]]). Running backs [[Larry Csonka]] and [[Mercury Morris]] became the first [[List of NFL 1,000-yard rushing duos|teammates to each rush for 1,000 yards]] in a season. [[Paul Warfield]] led the team in receptions and receiving yards, and [[Marlin Briscoe]] led the team in receiving touchdowns. The offensive line included future Hall of Famers [[Jim Langer]] and [[Larry Little]].100 Things Dolphins Fans Should Know and Do Before They Die, Armando Salguero, Triumph Books, Chicago, 2020, ISBN 978-1-62937-722-3, p. 70 The Dolphins' early-1970s defensive unit was termed the "No-Name Defense" by [[Dallas Cowboys]] head coach [[Tom Landry]], given its lack of high-profile players (the unit's only Hall of Famer, linebacker [[Nick Buoniconti]], achieved much of his success with the [[New England Patriots|Boston Patriots]] in the 1960s and was not inducted until 2001). The defense was led by Buoniconti, end [[Bill Stanfill]], tackle [[Manny Fernandez (American football)|Manny Fernandez]], and safeties [[Dick Anderson]] and [[Jake Scott]]. In all, nine Dolphins—Csonka, Morris, Warfield, Little, [[Norm Evans]], Buoniconti, Stanfill, Anderson, and Scott—were selected to the Pro Bowl, and Little, Morrall, Stanfill, and Anderson were named [[1972 All-Pro Team|first-team All-Pro]].{{cite web|title=1972 Miami Dolphins Roster|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/1972_roster.htm|publisher=Sports Reference, LLC|work=Pro-Football-Reference|access-date=September 6, 2011|archive-date=August 16, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110816171314/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/1972_roster.htm|url-status=live}} The Dolphins went 14–0 in the regular season, the best record in the league by three games, and won all three postseason games to finish 17–0. Three other teams, the [[Chicago Bears]] in [[1934 Chicago Bears season|1934]] and [[1942 Chicago Bears season|1942]] and the New England Patriots in [[2007 New England Patriots season|2007]], reached the NFL's title game undefeated and untied, but all three lost the championship. Four other teams, the [[Akron Pros]] in [[1920 Akron Pros season|1920]], the [[Canton Bulldogs]] in [[1922 Canton Bulldogs season|1922]] and [[1923 Canton Bulldogs season|1923]], and the [[Green Bay Packers]] in [[1929 Green Bay Packers season|1929]], won the NFL championship with an undefeated record, but all recorded at least one tie. The [[1985 Chicago Bears season|1985 Chicago Bears]]' bid for an undefeated season was snapped by the Dolphins in their game 13 [[Monday Night Football]] meeting.{{cite web |last1=Oyefusi |first1=Daniel |title=1985 Dolphins forever connected to perfect 1972 team after giving 12-0 Bears first and only loss |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/sports/nfl/miami-dolphins/article268062487.html |website=Miami Herald |access-date=January 18, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221102122522/https://www.miamiherald.com/sports/nfl/miami-dolphins/article268062487.html |archive-date=November 2, 2022 |date=November 2, 2022}}{{cite web |last1=Biggs |first1=Brad |title=1985 Bears-Dolphins on Monday Night Football: A perfect season evaporated |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2015/11/29/1985-bears-dolphins-on-monday-night-football-a-perfect-season-evaporated/ |website=Chicago Tribune |access-date=January 18, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240907151411/https://www.chicagotribune.com/2015/11/29/1985-bears-dolphins-on-monday-night-football-a-perfect-season-evaporated/ |archive-date=September 7, 2024 |date=29 November 2015}} Miami led the league in total offense, total defense, scoring offense, and scoring defense, the only team ever to do so. On August 20, 2013, four decades after the perfect season, President [[Barack Obama]] hosted the surviving members of the 1972 Dolphins, noting they "never got their [[White House]] visit."{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Er3z00blcec&t=1m |title=President Obama Honors the 1973 Super Bowl Champion Miami Dolphins |publisher=YouTube.com/user/whitehouse |date=August 20, 2013 |access-date=August 21, 2013 |archive-date=October 22, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131022081725/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Er3z00blcec&t=1m |url-status=live}}{{cite web|title=Perfect 1972 Miami Dolphins Team Going to the White House|url=http://www.sportsmedia101.com/miamidolphins/2013/08/13/perfect-1972-miami-dolphins-team-going-to-the-white-house/|access-date=August 15, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130818011355/http://www.sportsmedia101.com/miamidolphins/2013/08/13/perfect-1972-miami-dolphins-team-going-to-the-white-house/|archive-date=August 18, 2013|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} Fifty years later, on October 23, 2022, the 1972 Dolphins were honored at halftime during a [[Sunday Night Football on NBC|Sunday Night Football]] game featuring the [[2022 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]] and [[2022 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]], the same matchup that occurred for the 1972 [[AFC Championship Game]]. For the 50th anniversary celebration, the Dolphins wore throwback uniforms as well as patches bearing a classic Dolphins logo, the number 50, and the years 1972 and 2022.{{cite web|url=https://sports.nbcsports.com/2022/10/23/the-perfect-nfl-season-1972-miami-dolphins-set-to-celebrate-50th-anniversary-on-sunday-night-football/|publisher=NBC Sports|title=The perfect NFL season: 1972 Miami Dolphins set to celebrate 50th anniversary tonight on Sunday Night Football|date=October 23, 2022|access-date=October 23, 2022|archive-date=October 30, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221030053813/https://sports.nbcsports.com/2022/10/23/the-perfect-nfl-season-1972-miami-dolphins-set-to-celebrate-50th-anniversary-on-sunday-night-football/|url-status=dead}} The 1972 Dolphins ranked number 1 on the 100 greatest teams of all time by the NFL on its 100th anniversary.{{cite web|title=NFL Top 100 Teams|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nfl-top-100-teams.htm|publisher=Pro Football Reference}}{{cite web|title=100 Greatest Teams: Numbers 100-1 SUPERCUT|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6qzU600OwVc|work=NFL.com}} ==Background== The Miami Dolphins franchise was founded in 1966 under head coach [[George Wilson (American football coach)|George Wilson]]. Wilson led the Dolphins to just fifteen wins in four seasons before being fired and replaced by [[Baltimore Colts]] head coach [[Don Shula]]. Despite his poor record, many of Wilson's player acquisitions contributed to the Dolphins' success in the early 1970s. [[Howard Schnellenberger]] as offensive coordinator, [[Bill Arnsparger]] (who had served as defensive line coach under Shula in Baltimore) as defensive coordinator, [[Carl Taseff]] as offensive backs coach, [[Monte Clark]] as offensive line coach, and [[Mike Scarry]] as defensive line coach, and retained defensive backs coach [[Tom Keane]] from Wilson's staff; each of these coaches remained with the team through 1972. In the [[1970 NFL draft|1970 draft]] and ensuing free agency period, Shula added cornerback [[Tim Foley (defensive back)|Tim Foley]], safety [[Jake Scott]], guard [[Bob Kuechenberg]], and future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame|Hall of Fame]] center [[Jim Langer]]. In Shula's [[1970 Miami Dolphins season|first season]], the Dolphins went 10–4 and reached the playoffs for the first time. Miami returned to the playoffs in [[1971 Miami Dolphins season|1971]] and defeated the [[1971 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] in the longest game in NFL history to secure the franchise's first playoff victory. The Dolphins shut out the [[1971 Baltimore Colts season|Baltimore Colts]], Shula's former team, to reach [[Super Bowl VI]], where they lost 24–3 to [[1971 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas]]. Leypoldt then kicked a 34-yard field goal, allowing the Bills to lead 13–7 at halftime.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/74698336/panama-city-news-herald/|title=Dolphins Cop Squeaker|date=October 23, 1972|newspaper=Panama City News-Herald|page=2B|access-date=March 30, 2021|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=May 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502030459/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/74698336/panama-city-news-herald/|url-status=live}} {{free access}} Dolphins tackle [[Manny Fernandez (American football)|Manny Fernandez]] strip-sacked Bills quarterback [[Dennis Shaw]] at the Buffalo 10-yard line on the first play of the third quarter. A few minutes after this transpired, Dolphins cornerback [[Curtis Johnson (cornerback)|Curtis Johnson]] blocked a punt by [[Spike Jones (American football)|Spike Jones]] of the Bills. After the Dolphins were penalized four times on that drive (a loss of 33 yards), Garo Yepremian kicked a 54-yard field goal, the longest in franchise history until [[Pete Stoyanovich]]'s 59-yard field goal in [[1989 Miami Dolphins season|1989]].{{cite news|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/11/12/Dan-Marino-threw-three-touchdown-passes-and-rookie-Pete/4818626850000/|title=Dan Marino threw three touchdown passes and rookie Pete...|author=Dave Raffo|date=November 12, 1989|newspaper=United Press International|access-date=March 30, 2021|archive-date=May 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502030525/https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/11/12/Dan-Marino-threw-three-touchdown-passes-and-rookie-Pete/4818626850000/|url-status=live}} The fourth quarter began with a 45-yard field goal by Leypoldt, cutting Miami's lead to 17–16. Later, the Bills capped off a touchdown-scoring drive with a six-yard pass from quarterback [[Mike Taliaferro]] to fullback [[Jim Braxton]]. ''Dolphins 14–7.'' |stats= '''Top passers''' *MIA – [[Bob Griese]] – 8/11, 88 yards, TD, INT *WAS – [[Billy Kilmer]] – 14/28, 104 yards, 3 INT '''Top rushers''' *MIA – [[Larry Csonka]] – 15 rushes, 112 yards *WAS – [[Larry Brown (running back)|Larry Brown]] – 22 rushes, 72 yards '''Top receivers''' *MIA – [[Paul Warfield]] – 3 receptions, 36 yards *WAS – [[Roy Jefferson]] – 5 receptions, 50 yards }} The Dolphins advanced to their second consecutive Super Bowl appearance, this time against the [[1972 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] at the [[Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum]] on January 14, 1973. Washington was favored by 1 point, despite Miami entering the game undefeated and the Redskins having three regular season losses.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197301140mia.htm|title=Super Bowl VII - Washington Redskins vs. Miami Dolphins - January 14th, 1973|publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=December 22, 2022}} Super Bowl VII quickly became a defensive battle between both teams, with the Dolphins and Redskins each starting with two drives that ended with punts. However, in the waning minutes of the first quarter, Miami engineered a scoring drive capped by a 28-yard touchdown pass from Griese to Twilley. On Washington's subsequent drive, [[Jake Scott]] intercepted [[Billy Kilmer]]'s pass. But the Dolphins failed to capitalize and both teams exchanged punts, while Kilmer threw another interception to [[Nick Buoniconti]], who then returned the ball for 32 yards, with two minutes remaining in the half. Miami took advantage this time and scored on a one-yard rush by Kiick. The Dolphins held a 14–0 lead at halftime. On the opening drive of the third quarter, the Redskins advanced as far as the Dolphins 17-yard line, before [[Manny Fernandez (American football)|Manny Fernandez]] sacked Kilmer on third down for a loss of eight yards. [[Curt Knight]]'s subsequent field goal attempt of 32 yards missed. The game then continued to be a defensive battle between the two teams. Both teams then exchanged punts again, while Griese was intercepted by [[Brig Owens]] late in the third quarter. Just over halfway through the fourth quarter, the Redskins again drove far into Dolphins territory. However, Scott intercepted another pass from Kilmer. Subsequently, Miami's next drive stalled at Washington's 34-yard line. Redskins defensive lineman [[Bill Brundige]] blocked Yepremian's 42-yard field goal attempt. Yepremian then tried to throw a pass, but the ball was instead caught by Washington cornerback [[Mike Bass]], who ran the other way to cut the Dolphins lead to 14–7. This play is sometimes referred to as "Garo's Gaffe". Both teams each had one more drive, but neither of them resulted in a score. Thus, Dolphins won Super Bowl VII by a score of 14–7. ==Awards and honors== * [[NFL Coach of the Year Award|Coach of the Year]] – [[Don Shula]] * [[NFL Comeback Player of the Year Award|Comeback Player of the Year]] – [[Earl Morrall]] * [[Super Bowl Most Valuable Player]] – [[Jake Scott]] ==Urban legend== There is an urban legend that every season, whenever the last remaining undefeated NFL team loses its first game, all the surviving members of the 1972 Miami Dolphins open bottles of champagne in celebration. Coach Don Shula tried to play down the myth by saying that two players, [[Dick Anderson]] and [[Nick Buoniconti]], who live near each other, sometimes have a toast together.{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/columns/story?columnist=wojciechowski_gene&id=2750571 |title=ESPN – Shoes ... The Jaw ... by any name, Shula still the king – Columnist |publisher=ESPN |date=February 1, 2007 |access-date=September 3, 2012 |archive-date=October 22, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022063013/http://sports.espn.go.com/espn/columns/story?columnist=wojciechowski_gene&id=2750571 |url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=http://www.snopes.com/sports/football/miami72.asp |title=Urban Legends Reference Pages: 1972 Miami Dolphins Toast First Losses by Undefeated Teams |date=18 December 2005 |publisher=Snopes.com |access-date=September 3, 2012}} However, they occasionally had [[Diet Coke]]s together, such as in 2005 when Bob Griese and Shula watched the [[2005 San Diego Chargers season|Chargers]] win over the [[2005 Indianapolis Colts season|Colts]], the last undefeated team [[2005 NFL season|that season]].{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/109805821/edmonton-journal/|title=Mixed feelings from class of '72|page=D6|date=December 19, 2005|agency=Associated Press|newspaper=Edmonton Journal|access-date=September 19, 2022|via=Newspapers.com}} {{free access}} The NFL capitalized on the legend during a commercial that aired during [[Super Bowl LIII]] commemorating the 100th year of the NFL. The commercial featured "44 of the greatest NFL athletes" at a formal dinner event with the attendees dressed in [[black tie]]. Cacophony breaks out, and three members of the 1972 Dolphins, Larry Little, Paul Warfield, Larry Csonka, are shown casually sitting at a table together uniquely dressed in aqua-colored formal coats, and all three are drinking champagne, laughing at the chaos happening around them.[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tJjiIuH1VnY&t=44s The 100-Year Game | SBLIII] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502030459/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tJjiIuH1VnY&t=44s |date=2021-05-02}} (posted to the NFL official YouTube channel on Feb 3, 2019) ==The perfect season== {{main|Perfect season}} [[File:Dolphins Honor Roll3.jpg|thumb|right|The 1972 team on the [[Miami Dolphins Honor Roll]]]] The 1972 Miami Dolphins were the first team to execute a perfect regular season in the post-merger NFL. They are the only team in NFL history to go undefeated and untied in the regular season and postseason. After their loss to [[1971 Dallas Cowboys season|the Dallas Cowboys]] in [[Super Bowl VI]] (Miami's only loss during calendar year 1972), Don Shula had vowed to not only reach the Super Bowl again but to win it. He forced the team to watch film of the loss twice while at training camp. Shula would later go on to say: {{blockquote| I think that's when we all came together for what was going happen for the next two years. What I stressed in the locker room was that we wanted to make sure this wouldn't happen again. Our goal was not to go to the Super Bowl but to win it.{{Cite book|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=-0ukAS0WhtAC&q=did+don+shula+make+his+team+watch+the+super+bowl+loss&pg=PA56|title = The Ultimate Super Bowl Book: A Complete Reference to the Stats, Stars, and Stories Behind Football's Biggest Game--and Why the Best Team Won - Second Edition|isbn = 9781610586696|last1 = McGinn|first1 = Bob|date = September 15, 2012|access-date = October 24, 2020|archive-date = November 18, 2020|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201118001000/https://books.google.com/books?id=-0ukAS0WhtAC&q=did+don+shula+make+his+team+watch+the+super+bowl+loss&pg=PA56|url-status = live}}}} An enduring controversy is based on the argument that the 1972 Dolphins played a soft schedule not possible under the current scheduling formula.{{cite web |last=Moulton |first=David |url=http://www.naplesnews.com/news/2008/feb/03/david-moulton-final-salute-1972-dolphins/ |title=David Moulton: A final salute to the 1972 Dolphins " Naples Daily News |publisher=Naplesnews.com |access-date=September 3, 2012 |archive-date=February 5, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080205084528/http://www.naplesnews.com/news/2008/feb/03/david-moulton-final-salute-1972-dolphins/ |url-status=dead}} Prior to the implementation of position scheduling in 1978, opponents were set by the NFL on a rotating basis.Urena, Ivan; ''Pro Football Schedules: A Complete Historical Guide from 1933 to the Present'', pp. 10-12 {{ISBN|0786473517}} The Dolphins' 1972 regular-season opponents posted an aggregate winning percentage of .397, and only two had winning records for that season (both the [[1972 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] and [[1972 New York Giants season|New York Giants]] finished 8–6). However, this does not constitute any record; [[1975 Minnesota Vikings season|the 1975 Minnesota Vikings]], who began 10–0 and finished 12–2, played 14 opponents with an average winning percentage of .332, and nine of their games were against teams 4–10 or worse.{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/min/1975.htm |title=1975 Minnesota Vikings |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |access-date=2018-03-30 |archive-date=2018-02-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202130559/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/min/1975.htm |url-status=live}} Also in finishing 14-0, the Dolphins outscored opponents an aggregate 385-171, but this was not as one-sided as the [[1968 Baltimore Colts season|1968 Baltimore Colts]], whom Shula had coached and Morrall had played for, and who scored more points (402) and gave up fewer (144). The [[1969 Minnesota Vikings season|1969 Vikings]] also had a greater point differential of 246 points. Both the [[Super Bowl III|Colts]] and [[Super Bowl IV|Vikings]] went to the Super Bowl, but lost. The Dolphins were beneficiaries of a weak AFC East that saw the [[1972 Baltimore Colts season|Colts]] lapse from a perennial contender into a three-year stretch in which they would win only 11 games; a [[1972 Buffalo Bills season|Bills]] team yet to find its legs with [[O. J. Simpson]] and the return of coach [[Lou Saban]]; a dysfunctional [[1972 New England Patriots|Patriots]] organization that had little to no talent to surround former No. 1 overall draft choice [[Jim Plunkett]]; and a [[1972 New York Jets season|Jets]] squad with a porous defense, offsetting the benefits of [[Joe Namath]] remaining healthy throughout the season and an emerging [[John Riggins]] in the running game. Miami also caught a scheduling break by facing an [[1972 Houston Oilers season|Oilers]] team that was in the midst of back-to-back 1–13 seasons, [[1972 San Diego Chargers season|a Chargers]] team beginning a run of four consecutive seasons in the AFC West cellar, and a [[1972 St. Louis Cardinals (NFL) season|Cardinals]] team that appeared to lack direction by rotating its starting quarterbacks instead of giving the job full-time to [[Jim Hart (American football)|Jim Hart]]. The Dolphins also caught the [[1972 Minnesota Vikings season|Vikings]] in the midst of a massive transformation following the return of [[Fran Tarkenton]], missing the playoffs for the only time between 1968 and 1978, finishing 7–7. The NFL's rules at the time forced the undefeated Dolphins (14–0) to play the Steelers (11–3) in Pittsburgh for the AFC Championship Game. Subsequent rule changes have since changed the playoff structure so that this would never happen again. Since the 1975 season, teams that have won their division and have had a superior record than their opponent (as was the case with the 1972 Dolphins when they faced the Steelers) would play their postseason games at home. The 1972 Dolphins consisted mostly of the same core of players that it possessed from 1970 through 1974 and was the most dominant NFL team during that stretch. In those five seasons, the Dolphins reached the playoffs all five years, won three AFC Championships, two Super Bowls and went undefeated and untied while winning the Super Bowl in 1972. They posted a record of 65–15–1, and were also the fastest franchise to win a Super Bowl after franchise inception and joining the NFL (seven years after starting in the AFL, three years after becoming a member of the NFL). ==Television coverage== Fans in the Miami area could not view the team's home games on television, as 1972 was the final year in which all NFL home games were blacked out on local television even if the stadium had sold out. To view the team's home games, Dolphins fans in the Miami-Dade area (as well as [[Broward County, Florida|Broward]] and [[Palm Beach County, Florida|Palm Beach]] counties) would have to attend home games in person or travel to outside markets such as Orlando, Tampa, Gainesville and Jacksonville to watch the games on television. [[NFL on CBS|CBS]] did not televise a Dolphins game in 1972. Miami's only home game vs. an NFC opponent (vs. the Cardinals) was selected for ABC's ''[[Monday Night Football]]'', and was the team's only Monday night game. NBC was the network for all other Dolphins games. [[Super Bowl VII]] was the first game to be televised in the market of origin under new rules that would come into effect the following season requiring games to be sold out within 72 hours of kickoff time to be aired in the market of origin (these blackout rules were lifted in 2015). As all Super Bowls (except [[Super Bowl I]]) have sold out, none have been blacked out since. ==2013 White House visit== [[File:Potus-1973-dolphins.jpg|thumb|right|President Obama honoring the 1972 team at the White House in 2013]] Four decades later, on August 20, 2013, the team was invited by President Barack Obama to visit the White House.
